title: The Vietnamese martyrs
hookLine: 117 martyrs from the 1700s and 1800s, most of them laypeople
carry: full of joy, and not alone

lines: STEP ON IT AND GO HOME.
cards: Soldiers stand around a wooden cross laid flat in the dirt of a courtyard. A prisoner is led in, a farmer, or a catechist, or a mother with children waiting at home, and told: walk across it, step on it, and you can go.
Tradition says this test was used again and again in Vietnam's persecutions. It asks for one step. Not a speech, not a signature.
Just a foot on two pieces of wood. Today, the people who wouldn't take that step.

teach.h: FARMERS, PRIESTS, A MOTHER, A SOLDIER.
teach.b: First, who they were. The Catholic faith in Vietnam was carried by missionaries, and by Vietnamese catechists who taught in the villages.
When rulers turned against it, Christians were hunted, churches were destroyed, and families hid their priests.

The martyrs the Church honors together include Vietnamese priests like Andrew Dung-Lac, Spanish and French bishops and missionaries, catechists, a soldier, a doctor, fishermen and farmers, and Agnes Le Thi Thanh, a mother who sheltered priests.
For them, the choice came down to that cross in the dirt. Refusing it meant prison, beatings, and often death. Third, a letter.
Paul Le Bao Tinh, a Vietnamese priest, wrote from his prison cell to young seminarians. He described chains, hunger and cruelty, and said the prison was like a picture of hell.
Then he said he was not alone: Christ was with him, and he was full of joy.
He asked them to pray for him, so he could stay faithful. Fourth, witnesses.

teach.h: WHO THEN SHALL SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF CHRIST?
teach.b: Saint Paul asks, in Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?"

And in Acts, Jesus tells his followers: "you shall be witnesses unto me." The Church calls its martyrs witnesses, the word Acts uses here. Pope John Paul II declared these Vietnamese martyrs saints together.
Vietnam's Catholics still keep their feast, and their names.

how: The Church keeps the memorial of Saint Andrew Dung-Lac and companions, and Vietnamese Catholic communities, in Vietnam and abroad, honor the martyrs with Masses, processions and shrines.

o: a French bishop who founded Vietnam's first seminary
a Vietnamese priest martyred in the persecutions
a Vietnamese emperor who ended the persecutions

games.q: the Vietnamese martyrs — tap the pairs.
p: step on it and go free

s: the Vietnamese martyrs were all European missionaries
they include Vietnamese priests, catechists, a soldier, farmers and a mother, with European bishops and missionaries.
Paul Le Bao Tinh wrote from prison that he was not alone
he described chains and hunger, and said Christ was with him.
in Acts, Jesus calls his followers witnesses
"you shall be witnesses unto me." the Church calls its martyrs witnesses.

games.q: you're a Vietnamese Catholic under arrest. soldiers lay a cross on the ground: step on it, and you can go home. what do you do?
o: step on it quickly and go home to your family.
promise to step on it tomorrow, to buy time.
games.why: the martyrs the Church honors refused, and faced prison, beatings and death for it.

practice: Picture a village church in Vietnam on a Sunday morning: motorbikes outside, children on the steps, the bell ringing.
Then widen it to the cities, the rice fields, the coast, families scattered around the world, and if you know a Vietnamese person, bring their face to mind.
If you pray, pray for Vietnam's Catholics and for all who suffer for their faith today; if not, simply wish the people of Vietnam well.

wordCard.voice: Andrew Dung-Lac. A Vietnamese priest martyr, among the catechists, mothers, soldiers and farmers who died rather than step on the cross in Vietnam's persecutions.

orig.note: Greek: a witness, the word Acts uses when Jesus says you shall be witnesses unto me.

carryVoice: Your line: full of joy, and not alone. Those words came out of a prison cell. See you tomorrow.
